content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is a condition where a significant number of bacteria are present in the urine without the typical symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI). Normally, urine is sterile, and the presence of bacteria in the absence of symptoms is not considered an infection unless specific thresholds are met. For instance, pyuria, defined as the presence of more than 10 leukocytes per cubic millimeter, is not classified as asymptomatic bacteriuria unless the bacterial count exceeds 10⁵ colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter. The pathogenesis of asymptomatic bacteriuria involves two primary mechanisms: microbial virulence and host factors. Escherichia coli is the most common causative organism. The condition is more prevalent in the elderly, with its frequency increasing with age. It is also slightly more common in Black populations. Risk factors for asymptomatic bacteriuria are similar to those for symptomatic bacteriuria and include pregnancy, aging, diabetes mellitus, sexual intercourse, use of diaphragms with spermicides, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), renal stones, spinal cord injuries, hemodialysis, indwelling urethral catheters, and genitourinary abnormalities. Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria is recommended only in specific populations where it is associated with preventable adverse outcomes, such as symptomatic UTIs, progression to chronic kidney disease or hypertension, development of urinary tract cancer, or reduced survival. These populations include pregnant women, individuals undergoing urologic procedures like transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), and post-renal transplant patients. In most cases, asymptomatic bacteriuria resolves spontaneously without treatment, and active treatment is not required unless the individual is pregnant, undergoing a renal transplant, or scheduled for a urinary tract procedure. In pregnant women, asymptomatic bacteriuria detected early in pregnancy carries a small risk of complications such as low birth weight or pyelonephritis. Most cases resolve postpartum. Diagnosis is based on urine culture results obtained using methods that minimize contamination and limit the time between sample collection and testing to avoid false positives due to bacterial growth. For asymptomatic women, two consecutive clean-catch urine specimens with the same organism at counts of ≥10⁵ CFU/mL are required for diagnosis. In men, a single clean-catch specimen with ≥10⁵ CFU/mL suffices. For catheterized individuals, ≥10² CFU/mL of a single organism in a catheterized specimen is diagnostic. The natural history of asymptomatic bacteriuria is generally benign, and complications are rare. However, in pregnancy, untreated cases may lead to symptomatic UTIs, preterm birth, low birth weight, or pyelonephritis later in pregnancy. The prognosis is excellent, with complete resolution following appropriate treatment in indicated cases. Treatment is not recommended for otherwise healthy individuals unless associated with a UTI. Exceptions include pregnant women, individuals undergoing transurethral prostatic resection, and post-renal transplant patients. Pregnant women should be screened for bacteriuria early in pregnancy and treated if results are positive. Antibiotic regimens for pregnant women include nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, cephalexin, fosfomycin, or trimethoprim (after the first trimester). Follow-up is essential due to the high recurrence rate, with urine cultures performed one week after therapy and monthly until delivery. For patients with indwelling urethral catheters, screening and treatment are not recommended unless bacteriuria persists 48 hours after catheter removal. Prophylaxis may be considered for urological procedures. Surgical intervention is not indicated for managing asymptomatic bacteriuria. In summary, asymptomatic bacteriuria is a condition that requires careful consideration of the clinical context. While treatment is unnecessary in most cases, specific populations benefit from screening and management to prevent complications.
